l: thirty years' truce, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: After ten years of war, the Athenians and Lacedemonians conclude the Thirty Years' Peace, a truce and peace agreement.

l: Syracusan war against Trinacria, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a war [by the Syracusans against Trinacria] The Syracusans gathered forces from Syracuse and their confederates to conquer Trinacria. The war ended with the defeat and destruction of Trinacria and the enslavement of its inhabitants.

l: battle between Syracuse and Trinacria, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a bloody battle [won by the Syracusans] In a bloody battle, the Trinacrians made a resolute resistance but were hard pressed and all died on the spot. The wounded killed themselves rather than become captives, and the Syracusans won the victory.

l: Corinthian war, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: A war between Corinth and Corcyra arising from conflict over Epidamnus; as both prepared larger fleets and Athens joined Corcyra, it contributed to Potidea's revolt. Another account places fighting around Corinth in an eight-year struggle involving Lacedaemonians, Boeotians, Athenians, Argives, and Corinthians.

l: Epidamnus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: A colony of Corcyra and Corinth, Epidamnus is disputed as Corinth’s metropolis; civil conflict brings expulsions, an Illyrian-backed siege, and appeals to Corcyra then Corinth.

l: Corinthian war at sea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_won_by Corcyra [in the first naval battle] Corinth and Corcyra built and assembled fleets for renewed fighting after Corinth's first defeat. In the later battle, Corinth had 150 ships and Corcyra 120, but Athenian ships arrived and helped Corcyra win; Corinth then avoided another engagement in harbor.

l: Volsci, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a people [formerly strong and powerful] The Volsci took advantage of Rome's weakness after the Gallic attack and raised arms against the Romans. They attacked the Roman camp but were surrounded and almost entirely destroyed after Marcus Furius struck their rear.

l: Campanians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Campanians, a colony out of Italy hired by the Agrigentines, had served under Amilcar guarding hill Athenea; during famine they demanded bread, then after the Syracusan fleet’s defeat accepted fifteen talents and defected to the Carthaginians.

l: Athenian alliance with Corcyra, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a military alliance [naval assistance to Corcyra] After hearing appeals from both Corcyra and Corinth, Athens decided to join Corcyra. Athens first sent ten ships and later sent twenty more, whose arrival helped the Corcyreans win the naval battle.

l: Potidea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Potidea, a Corinthian colony, was the first city to defect from Athens after Corinthian and Perdiccas’s urging. Athens defeated forces near Pallene and besieged it. After surrendering, its inhabitants settled among the Chalcidicans in Thrace, and Athens colonized the city and surrounding country.

l: Perdiccas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a king [of Macedonia] Perdiccas, king of Macedonia, was opposed by Sitalces, who intended to restore Amyntas to his father's kingdom. He eventually made peace with Sitalces and sealed the agreement by marriage.

l: Chalcidica, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: participates_in Potidean revolt [against Athens] Chalcidica was a target of the Athenians and Sitalces. Its Greek cities joined a broader confederacy because they feared an invasion by the powerful Thracians.

l: Potidean revolt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a revolt [against Athens] The Potidean revolt was encouraged by Corinth and by Perdiccas, who was hostile to Athens. Athens responded by sending a fleet and army to destroy the rebels' country and storm the city.

l: Battle near Pallene, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: A great battle was fought in the isthmus near Pallene between the Athenians and forces supporting Potidea. The Athenians won and killed more than three hundred of the enemy.

l: Athenian siege of Potidea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: After the Athenian victory near Pallene, the siege of Potidea was formally established. Callias died in a later Athenian victory at Potidea, and Phormio succeeded him and continued the siege with repeated assaults.

l: Agis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Agis succeeds Archidamus as Lacedaemonian king and commands the Lacedemonians. Restrained by Pharax at Mantinea, he offers battle against Argos but is stopped by a truce; spared after near execution, he gains ten advisers. He later attacks Athens, loses cavalry, abandons the siege, and returns to Peloponnesus.

l: Phormio, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Phormio succeeds Callias as Athenian general after Callias is killed at Potidea, renews its siege, and faces prolonged resistance. Made admiral, he commands twenty ships at Naupactus, occupies Criseus to block the Lacedaemonians, wins at Rhion, captures ships, and drives their fleet toward Corinth.

l: the Peloponnesian War, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Peloponnesian War was a war between Athens and Lacedaemon, their allies, and opposing confederates. It began after disputes involving Megara and wider rivalry between Athens and Sparta. Its course included invasions of Attica and Peloponnesus; the siege of Potidea; naval fighting at Rhion; Athenian campaigns in Sicily and Lesbos; the destruction of Plataea; plague and famine at Athens; fighting across western Greece, Boeotia, Megara, and Thrace; the fortification of Pylos; capture of the Sphacterian prisoners; Brasidas’s expansion around Amphipolis; and the Boeotian victory at Delium. After ten years, Athens and Lacedaemon made a fifty-year peace requiring prisoners’ release and restoration of captured cities, but conflict later renewed amid shifting alliances, with Athens preparing war against the Syracusans in Sicily. The final phase brought political change at Athens, naval battle between Sestos and Abydos, and weakening on both sides. It ended when the Athenian fleet was defeated, Athens was blockaded, and the city surrendered. The records variously give durations of twenty-two and twenty-seven years. It caused many murders and lamentable bloodshed, and left Lacedaemon sovereign by sea and land, able to organize governments in Greek cities.

l: Alcibiades, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Alcibiades is an Athenian, Pericles's underage nephew and ward, portrayed as noble, wealthy, eloquent, and skilled in martial affairs. Early on, he advised Pericles to evade an inquiry into entrusted money by pursuing a great war. He supported Argos, helped restore its democracy by expelling Lacedaemonian supporters, and became one of three generals sent against Syracuse, as well as the principal promoter of the Sicilian expedition. Accused at Athens over the mutilation of Minerva's statues and condemned to death in absentia with fellow fugitives, he escaped from Sicily and fled to Sparta. There he urged the Lacedaemonians to invade Athens and assist Syracuse, while avoiding revenge from both Syracusans and Athenians. While banished, he initially aided the Lacedaemonians, then prevented Pharnabazus from sending three hundred ships to them. Recalled by Athens, he became general and helped restore its fortunes through victories and support for troops. He commanded forces at Dardanium and Cyzicum, where deception helped defeat and pursue Mindarus; Athens sent thirty additional ships afterward. He gathered money and Thracian aid, took Selymbria, captured Byzantium with Theramenes, and returned to Athens greatly admired. There he defended himself, recovered confiscated property, was absolved of condemnation and alleged profanation, and received full authority by sea and land. After defeating the Andrians, his position declined following the defeat at Notium, attributed to Antiochus's disobedience. He devastated Cuma, faced accusations of attacking a confederate city, yielded the fleet to Conon, and withdrew into self-imposed exile in Thrace, where he had friends Medocus and Seuthes. Seeking access to the Persian king after learning of Cyrus's plans, he was trapped in Phrygia, his lodging burned, and he was killed by fire and missiles.

l: Brasidas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Brasidas was a young, strong, courageous Spartan soldier, commander, admiral, and general. He won honor in Sparta by entering threatened Methone through Athenian forces and helping preserve it. At Pylos he forced his ship ashore and fought the Athenians despite severe wounds and losing his shield. He relieved Megara, led an expedition through Thessaly to Macedonia, gained Thracian communities for the Lacedaemonians, captured Amphipolis, Torone, and nearby places, and fortified Scione and Menda. He was killed fighting Cleon at Amphipolis among heaps of enemies.

l: plague of Athens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The plague of Athens spread amid crowding during the Lacedaemonian invasion, killed many people, weakened Athenians, and contributed to anger against Pericles.

l: siege of Potidea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: ends_in surrender of Potidea [because of extreme shortage of provisions] The siege of Potidea lasted through repeated assaults and caused heavy Athenian losses from fighting and disease. The besiegers lost more than a thousand men before Potidea surrendered on terms requiring all inhabitants to leave with only limited clothing.

l: siege of Plataea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Lacedaemonians maintained a long siege of Plataea and built walls, forts, and guards around the city. Some Plateans escaped to Athens, but the remainder surrendered and were executed, and Plataea was destroyed.

l: Athenian victory at Rhion, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: At Rhion, Phormio’s twenty Athenian ships defeated forty-seven Lacedaemonian ships, sank the admiral’s ship, captured twelve vessels, erected a trophy, and dedicated a ship to Neptune.

l: Sitalces, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Sitalces, king of Thrace, is just and kind to his subjects, and enlarges his dominions through valor and prudence. With annual revenue above a thousand talents, he commands more than 120,000 foot and 50,000 horse. Allied with the Athenians, he invades Macedonia against Perdiccas to restore Amyntas, then makes peace with Perdiccas, confirms it by marriage, and withdraws into Thrace.

l: Amyntas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a son [of Philip] Amyntas, the son of Philip, was brought with the Thracians as the intended king of Macedonia. His restoration was one of the reasons for Sitalces's invasion.

l: Gorgias, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Gorgias, an eloquent Leontine orator and ambassador, teaches rhetoric’s rules and persuades Athens to ally with the Leontines through an elaborate appeal for aid.

l: Eurymedon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a Athenian general Eurymedon arrived with Demosthenes and a large army from Athens, together with additional forces from Tholium and Messapia. He commanded the Athenian right wing in the first naval battle in Syracuse harbor, where he was mortally wounded and killed, and seven ships under his command were destroyed.

l: Sophocles, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Sophocles, son of Theophilus, was a tragedian who won eighteen stage victories and died at about ninety.

l: Paches, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Paches, son of Epiderus, commanded the Athenian forces sent to Lesbos. After joining the earlier army at Mitylene, he tightened the siege and attacked the city by sea and land.

l: Cleon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Cleon, an admiral of the Athenian fleet, led a large force in Thrace, took Torone, marched toward Scione and Amphipolis, fought Brasidas, and was killed at Amphipolis.

l: Marcus Manlius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a Roman defender [of the Capitol] Marcus Manlius hastened to defend the Capitol when the Gauls climbed its rock. He cut off one Gaul's hand and knocked another from the wall, causing the remaining Gauls to retreat and perish on the steep rock.

l: Chalcidicans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Chalcidicans joined the other Greeks in raising an army against Sitalces. They were also the people of Chalcidica whom the Athenians intended to attack with Sitalces's assistance.

l: Lesbians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The inhabitants of Lesbos revolt from Athenians after their cities’ inhabitants are brought to Mitylene, then ally with Lacedaemonians and promise many ships.

l: Mityleneans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Mityleneans defeat the Athenians in a sea-fight, endure an Athenian siege as countryside people seek refuge, then surrender after famine, warfare, and sedition.

l: Plateans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Plateans, inhabitants of Plataea, endure siege, shortages, and losses; some escape to Athens, while those surrendering Plataea are executed by Lacedaemonians.

l: Athenian expedition to Sicily, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Athenian expedition to Sicily was a military expedition, preceded by Athenian fleets sent to support Leontium and pursue wider designs; those forces raided the Lipari islands, fought near the Myleans, captured a Locrian castle, and returned after peace between Leontium and Syracuse. After appeals from the Leontines and Egestaeans, Athens approved a larger expedition against the Syracusans under Alcibiades, Nicias, and Lamachus. Accounts describe a large fleet and army, including 130 ships and 5,000 armed men, or more than 7,000 armed men. It travelled through Corcyra and Italy, captured Hyccara, occupied Catana, and began operations against Syracuse. Its intended policy was to enslave Selinus and Syracuse and impose tribute on other cities. Condemned as unjust, it ended in complete destruction: neither ship nor man returned, and its army and generals were left at Syracusan mercy.

l: Lesbian revolt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The revolt began when the inhabitants of Lesbos opposed Athenian measures that removed the inhabitants of its cities to Mitylene. The rebels sought Lacedaemonian support, but the Athenians sent forces under Paches, besieged Mitylene, and imposed their settlement after its surrender.

l: Demosthenes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Demosthenes was an Athenian general and admiral who commanded forces and fleets. In Acarnania he defeated Ambracian troops, though the Acarnanians would not join an assault on Ambracia. He fortified and defended Pylos against the Lacedaemonians and joined Hippocrates in an unsuccessful effort at Megara. Expected with a fleet and reinforcements, he later arrived in Sicily with Eurymedon, urged attack at Epipolae, then advocated retreat from Syracuse. After a naval defeat he proposed breaking the harbor blockade, led a division in retreat, and was captured.

l: Nicias, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Nicias is an Athenian admiral and general whose record centers on military command and his conflicted role in the Sicilian expedition. He led naval expeditions against Melos, Boeotia, Corinth, Cythera, and the Peloponnesian coast; won engagements against Corinthians; captured Cremmyon, Cythera, and Thyrea; fortified Methone; and later helped take Menda before besieging Scione. Though he opposed the expedition to Sicily from the beginning, warning that Athens could not safely fight Sparta while seeking Sicily, he was appointed one of three generals and commanded the siege of Syracuse. After Alcibiades fled and Lamachus was killed, he remained in command, requested reinforcements, and initially resisted abandoning the siege. He accepted retreat only later, then, being naturally superstitious, delayed after a lunar eclipse on soothsayers' advice. He led one division in the retreat, was captured with Demosthenes after the army's defeat, and was executed with the other generals.

l: Sphacteria, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Sphacteria is an island near Pylos at the harbor entrance; Spartans and allied elite soldiers occupied it until an Athenian fleet blockaded it and forced surrender.

l: Delium, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_fortified_by Athenians [with a wall under Hippocrates] Delium was occupied and fortified by Hippocrates and the Athenians near Oropus and the borders of Boeotia. The Boeotians later assaulted it, killed much of its garrison, captured 200 defenders, and forced the remaining Athenians to escape.

l: Pylos siege, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a siege [conducted by the Lacedaemonians against Pylos] The Lacedaemonians besieged Pylos with land forces and a fleet of forty-five ships, attacking the walls repeatedly while trying to block the harbor. The Athenians resisted, and the siege ended with the Lacedaemonians losing control of the Sphacterian island and surrendering its defenders.

l: Battle of Delium, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Battle between Athenians and Boeotians after Athens fortified Delium; Theban forces routed Athenian troops, who fled toward Oropus, Delium, and ships, securing a signal Boeotian victory.

l: capture of the Sphacterian prisoners, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a capture [by the Athenians after the Lacedaemonians surrendered] The Athenians captured 120 Spartans and 180 of their confederates after the soldiers on the Sphacterian island were starved and forced to submit. Cleon brought the prisoners bound to Athens, where their fate was made conditional on whether the Lacedaemonians ended the war.

l: fortification at Pylos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a wall [built by Demosthenes around naturally fortified Pylos] Demosthenes built a wall around Pylos in twenty days because the site was naturally strong and well supplied. The fortification survived repeated Lacedaemonian assaults and became the base from which the Athenians controlled the sea and threatened Laconia.

l: Sphacterian island, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Sphacterian island lay near the harbor of Pylos and was considered useful for securing the harbor and supporting the siege. Lacedaemonian and allied soldiers stationed there were cut off from supplies by the Athenian fleet and eventually surrendered.

l: Lamac​hus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Athenian general commanding ten ships, sent against Syracuse, lost ships near Cacheta, and was killed battling Gylippus and Syracusans.

l: Scione, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: defects_to the Lacedaemonians [under the protection of Brasidas] Scione defected from the Athenians to the Lacedaemonians and was placed under Brasidas's protection. It was besieged by Nicias and Nicostratus and later fiercely assaulted by Cleon, while its strong garrison defended it.

l: the battle of Amphipolis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_won_by the Lacedaemonians [after Brasidas and Cleon were killed] The battle of Amphipolis was fought between the Athenians under Cleon and the Lacedaemonians under Brasidas. Both generals were killed, the Lacedaemonians won, and the Athenians buried their dead under a truce.

l: the siege of Scione, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_conducted_by the Athenians [with continual assaults after surrounding the city with a wall] The siege of Scione began when Nicias and Nicostratus surrounded the city with a wall and repeatedly assaulted it. Scione's strong garrison, well supplied with necessities, defended the city and inflicted heavy losses on the besiegers.

l: Cumaeans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Cumeans defended their city and country when Alcibiades attacked and carried off prisoners. They defeated his force, recovered the captives, and brought a formal accusation against him at Athens for wasting a confederate city that had done them no injury.

l: Pharax, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Pharax, a Lacedaemonian councillor and admiral, commanded a fleet of one hundred and twenty ships, sailed from Rhodes to besiege Caunus, then withdrew to Rhodes before an approaching army.

l: Argive thousand, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Argive thousand were one thousand wealthy young soldiers trained at public expense. After fighting at Mantinea, they seized power in Argos, established an oligarchy, and were overthrown by popular insurrection.

l: Egestaeans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Egestaeans warred with Selinuntines over Sicilian boundaries, suffered heavy defeat, failed to gain regional aid, then sought Athenian intervention by displaying borrowed and private wealth.

l: Selinuntines, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Selinuntines are a group defined by territorial conflict and shifting alliances. They crossed their boundary with the Egestaeans, seized land, defeated them, and later fought Egesta again over disputed borders, rejecting Syracusan arbitration before suffering defeat by Egestaeans and allies. Allied with Carthaginians and joining Dionysius against Motya, they finally resisted Hannibal but were overwhelmed, with heavy deaths, captivity, and escapees to Agrigentum.

l: Mantinea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a Arcadian city [supported by confederates against the Lacedaemonians] Mantinea supported the Argives and faced the advancing Lacedaemonians with the youth of its city and allied forces. After the Lacedaemonians' victory, Mantinea was left without the Argive garrison and was forced under Lacedaemonian power.

l: Battle of Mantinea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a battle [between the Lacedaemonians and the Argives with their allies] At the Battle of Mantinea, the Argive thousand initially routed part of the opposing army, but the Lacedaemonians turned against them and surrounded them. Pharax ordered a passage opened, allowing the thousand Argive soldiers to escape, while the Lacedaemonians secured the victory.

l: Argive oligarchic coup, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Argive thousand and wealthy supporters overthrow democracy, establish aristocracy for eight months, then popular insurrection restores democracy.

l: democracy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_restored_in Argos [after the oligarchic regime was overthrown] Democracy in Argos was overthrown by the Argive thousand and their supporters. It was restored after a popular insurrection and later reinforced when Alcibiades banished those who favored the Lacedaemonians.

l: aristocracy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: An aristocracy was established in Argos by the Argive thousand after they seized the leading supporters of popular government. The arrangement lasted eight months before the people deposed its leaders and restored democracy.

l: league of Athens and Sparta, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Athens and Sparta privately formed a league that was both offensive and defensive, excluding the cities that had supported either side. Its provision allowing them to add to or remove from the agreed terms led other Greek cities to suspect plans for domination and to form a counter-alliance.

l: Hermocrates, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Hermocrates is a Syracusan general and assembly member, esteemed for service in the war against the Athenians. During the night assault on Epipolae, he led selected young men to aid Syracuse and helped drive out the Athenians; his later advice to deploy forces at night and block roads was rejected. In assembly he opposed harsh treatment of prisoners, urging moderation and humanity over victory by force. Though favored by Pharnabazus and commanding thirty-five ships for the Lacedaemonians, he was banished by a contrary Syracusan faction and forbidden to enter Syracuse. From Selinus, after support for recall and failed restoration, he built forces, raided Carthaginian territories, honored Syracusan dead from Himera, and sought return. He entered with three thousand armed men, but was killed at Syracuse with many accomplices.

l: Gylippus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Gylippus, a Lacedaemonian general sent to aid Syracuse, raised troops in Sicily, reinforced Syracuse, and helped lead resistance against the Athenians and recover Epipolae. He argued against sparing Athenian prisoners. Later, after taking three hundred talents, he was condemned to die for theft.

l: Egesta, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: seeks_protection_from Carthaginians [against the Selinuntines and Syracusans] Egesta feared that the Syracusans would retaliate for its earlier hostility and appealed to the Carthaginians after the Selinuntines encroached on disputed territory. With Carthaginian and Campanian assistance, its forces surprised and routed the Selinuntines, killing about a thousand.

l: Epipolae, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Epipolae is high land near Syracuse overlooking and capable of commanding the city. Its strategic value lay in controlling or pressuring Syracuse: Athenians seized it in night attacks, briefly held forts and built or used fortified positions, but Gylippus and the Syracusans defeated them and destroyed their works. Dionysius later chose it for major defensive fortification.

l: Alcibiades's flight from Sicily, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a flight [by Alcibiades after recall for trial] After Athens recalled Alcibiades to stand trial, he sailed from Catana but escaped at Thurii. He then fled from Italy to Sparta, while Athens condemned him and his fellow fugitives to death in their absence.

l: Athenians' Sicilian expedition, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Athenians' Sicilian expedition was an Athenian siege of Syracuse by sea and land. The Athenians seized Epipolae, fortified Labdalon and Polichna, and built walls to block the city and port; Nicias commanded its continuation. Although reinforcements arrived, Gylippus and Syracusan aid, a failed assault, plague, and naval defeats reversed the siege. The remaining forces abandoned their fleet, retreated by land, and suffered eighteen thousand deaths and seven thousand captures.

l: battle at Syracuse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The forces of Gylippus and the Syracusans fought the Athenians near Syracuse, and Lamachus was killed. Although the Athenians initially won the battle, the Syracusans later defeated them in an assault on the Athenian camp and Epipolae.

l: war between Lacedaemon and Athens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: lasts_for twelve years [the conflict continued after the Lacedaemonians broke their league with Athens] At the instigation of Alcibiades, the Lacedaemonians broke their league with Athens. The text states that the war between them continued for twelve years.

l: Athenian fleet, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_equipped_with 140 galleys [besides ships of burden and other ships] The Athenians equipped 140 galleys, in addition to ships for horses, provisions, and other necessities, for the expedition. The fleet sailed through the Ionian Sea and along the Italian coast to Sicily, later moved from Catana to the great port of Syracuse, and received further support from Athens.

l: Athenian army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: has_strength above seven thousand men at arms, slingers, and horsemen [including men sent by the confederates] The Athenian army included more than seven thousand armed men, slingers, and cavalry from the allied forces. It captured Hyccara, fought the Syracusans, occupied Epipolae, built siege works around Syracuse, and later withdrew to another position after losing Epipolae.

l: Syracusan officers, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: foresee Athenian movement toward the sea-shore [before the engagement] The Syracusan army was organized under Hermocrates, Sicanus, and Heraclides and fought the invading Athenians. It received reinforcements from Gylippus and other allies, defeated the Athenians at Epipolae, and helped demolish their walls and fortifications.

l: the Athenian democracy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Democracy was promoted by Athens in its allied cities and supported by the people of Corcyra. The democratic faction at Corcyra expelled its oligarchic opponents, while Theramenes restored democratic government at Paros. The Athenian democracy was abolished by a general vote after Lysander threatened Theramenes and pressured the Athenians. Its replacement was the government of the Thirty.

l: Decelea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Decelea is a strong place suitable for a garrison, seized and fortified by the Lacedemonians, giving the war its name.

l: sea-fight, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The first sea-fight involved eighty well-manned Syracusan ships and sixty Athenian ships; the Athenians sank eleven Syracusan ships after turning back to fight. A later sea-fight in the Great Haven favored the Syracusans, who used their stronger, lower forecastles to board and defeat the Athenian galleys.

l: fleet, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Athenians delayed further action while awaiting Demosthenes with a fleet. The Syracusans repeatedly challenged the Athenian fleet and eventually engaged it fully in the Great Haven.

l: gallies, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Athenians were assigned eighty galleys for the Sicilian expedition, and sixty took part in the first sea-fight. Their galleys were swift but had slender, high-built forecastles, while the Syracusan vessels had low, strongly built foredecks that could damage them at the first strike.

l: Athenian forts, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Athenian forts held money, naval preparations, and provisions; lightly guarded, they were seized by Syracusans during the sea-fight.

l: plague in the Athenian camp, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: A plague caused by nearby marshy ground breaks out in the Athenian army, spreads, kills many Athenians, and makes them regret not departing earlier.

l: Athenian night assault on Epipolae, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: A nighttime Athenian assault on Epipolae began with an unexpected attack by sea and land, taking forts and damaging the wall, but ended in defeat as darkness and unfamiliar passages dispersed troops, enabling Syracusan casualties.

l: lunar eclipse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: A lunar eclipse occurred on the night before the Athenians intended to sail. Nicias, who was superstitious and distressed by the plague, consulted soothsayers, who advised delaying the departure for three days.

l: first naval battle in Syracuse harbor, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: results_in Athenian loss [two thousand men and eighty galleys] In the first naval battle, the Syracusans used seventy-four galleys against eighty-six Athenian galleys. Eurymedon was killed, seven Athenian ships were destroyed, and the Athenians were driven into the shallows; the Athenians lost two thousand men and eighty galleys, while their land forces routed the Syracusans on shore.

l: second naval battle in Syracuse harbor, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: A naval battle attempting to break the Syracusan blockade: Athenians deployed 115 galleys against seventy-four Syracusan ships, their formation broke apart, and the Syracusans won, destroying sixty Athenian ships while losing eight and disabling eleven.

l: Athenian retreat from Syracuse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Athenian retreat from Syracuse, led by Nicias alongside Demosthenes, follows a second naval defeat, a divided march toward Catana, harassment and blocked passes, and surrender when trapped at the Asinarus.

l: Syracusan victory, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: results_in Athenian capture [including Demosthenes and Nicias] The Syracusan victory included the defeat of the Athenian fleet and the destruction of the Athenian army. The Syracusans killed eighteen thousand Athenians, captured seven thousand including Demosthenes and Nicias, and erected two trophies in celebration.

l: Syracuse's great haven, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_blocked_by Syracusan harbor blockade [to prevent Athenian escape by sea] Syracuse harbor became the scene of two major naval battles. Its shallows, fortifications, and blocked entrance prevented the Athenians from escaping and contributed to the destruction of their fleet.

l: Syracusan harbor blockade, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_made_of war galleys [joined and fastened together with chains] The Syracusans blocked the mouth of the harbor with boats, galleys, and other ships fastened together with iron chains. They also made a bridge-like barrier of connected vessels, preventing the Athenians from escaping by sea.

l: war galleys, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: are_used_by Athenians [for naval combat and escape] War galleys were central to both naval engagements. The Athenians used eighty-six galleys in the first battle and 115 in the second, while the Syracusans used seventy-four in each; many were destroyed, disabled, or captured amid ramming, grappling, fires, and fighting aboard the ships.

l: military strategy and escape, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Demosthenes favored returning to Athens and later proposed using the remaining ships to break the blockade, while Nicias favored abandoning the fleet and marching inland toward allied cities. The Athenians ultimately followed the land-retreat plan, but the Syracusans blocked the roads and trapped them at the Asinarus River.

l: Nicholaus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Nicholaus is an aged Syracusan elder, supported by servants, who lost two sons in war. Despite this loss, he urges mercy for Athenian prisoners, arguing clemency would bring Syracuse honour, peace, and moderation.

l: Athenian prisoners, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Athenian prisoners, surrendered captives and suppliants of the Syracusans, become the subject of a Syracuse assembly. Diocles urges severe punishment, while Hermocrates and Nicholaus urge mercy. They are depicted as either distressed suppliants or aggressors; most suffer harsh imprisonment, but some are released because of useful liberal education.

l: the assembly at Syracuse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: A deliberative civic body convenes after the Athenian defeat to decide the prisoners’ fate, weighing Diocles’ harsh decree against Hermocrates’ objection and Nicholaus’ plea for clemency.

l: the war between Athens and Syracuse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The war begins when the Athenians attack Syracuse without provocation, breaking or threatening the peace. It brings calamity, including the loss of Nicholaus’s two sons, and ends in a reversal: the Athenians’ Sicilian expedition is completely destroyed and the former besiegers of Syracuse become prisoners.

l: mercy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Mercy is debated after victory over Athenian prisoners. It is praised as honourable, useful, and able to create friendship, peace, gratitude, and praise; it is also urged because of Athens, compelled allies, and Nicias’s kindness. Gylippus rejects it, citing aggression and atrocities.

l: cruelty, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: causes rebellion [when rulers govern through fear] Cruelty toward surrendered prisoners is portrayed as dishonourable, imprudent, and contrary to the customs of the Greeks. Nicholaus warns that cruelty can provoke hatred, rebellion, and disgrace.

l: honour and glory, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Honour and glory are said to come from defeating the Athenians through mercy and humanity as well as through arms. Syracuse is urged to gain lasting praise by sparing the prisoners rather than seeking a brief satisfaction through their destruction.

l: Athenian generals, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: are_executed revenge and punishment [after capture by the Syracusans] The Athenian generals are held responsible for continuing the war and siege. They are put to death along with all their confederates after the Syracusans accept Diocles's advice.

l: the Sicilian expedition, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a the Athenian invasion of Sicily The Sicilian expedition was opposed by Nicias but promoted by Alcibiades and undertaken by the Athenians. It ended in defeat, the capture of the Athenian forces, and a debate over whether the survivors should be spared.

l: revenge and punishment, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The speech presents punishment as justified revenge for the Athenian invasion, intended enslavement, and destruction of other cities. The Syracusans ultimately execute the generals and confederates and imprison the Athenian citizens rather than release them.

l: slavery, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_planned_for Syracusans [in the Athenians' common assemblies] The Athenians had planned that the Syracusans and Selinuntines would be made slaves and that other Sicilians would pay tribute. Their own threatened enslavement is used as a reason to punish them, and the speech recalls that they had enslaved or destroyed others when victorious.

l: the Dioclean laws, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Dioclean laws were made for the Syracusans and were named after Diocles, although others helped formulate them. They imposed severe punishments for violations of justice, assigned fines proportionate to offenses, and were used by many Sicilian cities until Rome brought Sicily under its power.

l: the four hundred, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: favor oligarchy [over the former democracy] The four hundred were chosen by the Athenians to govern Athens after the Sicilian disaster, replacing the democracy with oligarchy. Their government failed to meet expectations, and their authority was later abolished.

l: oligarchy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Oligarchy is a form of government favored by the Lacedaemonians and imposed in cities hostile to them. Athenians adopted it in desperation, but the government of the four hundred failed and was abolished; elsewhere, it was removed and democracy restored.

l: Pharnabazus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Pharnabazus is a Persian lieutenant, lord-lieutenant, satrap, commander, and naval leader serving the Persian king. He receives Miletan democratic refugees at Clauda, prepares money and three hundred Phoenician ships for the Lacedaemonians, but sends the ships back after Alcibiades argues that their success would harm Persian interests. He supports Lacedaemonian operations at Dardanium, Cyzicum, and Claros, where his army is defeated and withdraws. After exposing Alcibiades’s planned disclosure to Artaxerxes, he denies him a passport and has him killed. He makes truces with Dercyllidas, raises forces, helps obtain a fleet under Conon, relieves Caunus, and commands the Persian fleet with Conon. After Cnidus, they invade Lacedaemonian allies and incite cities and islands to revolt.

l: the battle of Oropus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The battle of Oropus was fought between the Athenians and the Lacedaemonians after the Athenians sent a fleet of forty ships. The Lacedaemonians prevailed and captured twenty-two Athenian ships.

l: Theramenes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Theramenes was an Athenian commander and political figure described as sober, prudent, influential, just, and moderate. He served as a common soldier before commanding fleets and part of the right wing at Arginusae. He tried unsuccessfully to prevent the Boeotians from blocking the Euripus, restored democracy at Paros, fought with Chares and Thrasybulus at Claros, besieged Chalcedon, arranged its tribute, and joined Alcibiades against Byzantium. In Athens he helped abolish the four hundred, supported democracy, and advised recalling Alcibiades. After Arginusae he defended himself over the unburied dead. Though selected among the Thirty, he opposed both their establishment and their abuses, and was condemned and executed.

l: the recall of Alcibiades, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The recall of Alcibiades was supported by Theramenes and approved by the Athenians after Alcibiades helped prevent Persian naval support for the Lacedaemonians. Alcibiades was absolved, appointed a general, and expected to restore Athenian strength.

l: Mindarus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Mindarus, a Lacedaemonian admiral, commanded Peloponnesian fleets from Abydos, fought Athenians near Sestos and Abydos, refitted ships and sought reinforcements, aided Dorieus, captured Cyzicum, and was killed defending ships at Claros, prompting Peloponnesian flight.

l: Clearchus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Clearchus is a Laconian harmost and tyrant of Byzantium who commands large mercenary and Greek forces. Sent to govern Byzantium, he gathers mercenaries, kills magistrates and leading citizens, confiscates goods, and banishes others. Defeated by the Lacedaemonians at Porus, he escapes to Selymbria and then Ionia, where Cyrus makes him a general. He commands Peloponnesians, Lacedaemonians, and mercenaries in battle, orders a close attack, restrains pursuit, defeats the king's forces, and refuses to surrender Greek arms. Going to Tissaphernes with other commanders, he is seized and killed.

l: Theramenes's restoration of democracy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Theramenes's restoration of democracy occurred when the Athenians abolished the authority of the four hundred and returned to democratic government. His influence also contributed to the decision to recall Alcibiades.

l: the naval battle between Sestos and Abydos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: occurs_between Sestos [and Abydos] The naval battle between Sestos and Abydos was fought between the Athenian and Lacedaemonian fleets. The Athenians, aided by superior pilots and the arrival of twenty-five additional ships, defeated the Lacedaemonians, capturing many allied ships while losing five themselves.

l: Cyzicum, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Cyzicum is a place besieged and captured by Mindarus with Pharnabazus’s assistance, then reached by Athenians who trapped the Peloponnesian fleet in a decisive battle that killed Mindarus and routed the Spartans.

l: the Athenian fleet, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Athenian fleet, more skilled in naval affairs and containing most Athenian men, gathered at Samos, trained, pursued and defeated the Lacedaemonian fleet, captured ships, and operated at Cyzicus and Samos.

l: the Lacedaemonian fleet, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Lacedaemonian fleet under Mindarus sailed to the Hellespont and fought the Athenians between Sestos and Abydos. Although it initially numbered eighty-eight ships and included Syracusan and other allied vessels, it was defeated and lost numerous ships.

l: Carthaginian war, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a war The Carthaginian war began when Egesta and Selinuntum separately sought aid from Carthage and Syracuse after their first battle. Hannibal was given overall responsibility for preparing the Carthaginian forces.

l: Dardanium, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Dardanium was where Dorieus landed his men and positioned his ships against the attacking Athenians. The Lacedaemonians later fled from the battle there after Alcibiades signaled the Athenians.

l: Battle at Dardanium, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Sea battle between Athenians and Lacedaemonians: Thrasybulus and Thrasyllus fought Mindarus's larger fleet until Alcibiades arrived, prompting flight; Athenians captured ten ships before a storm ended pursuit.

l: Corcyrian sedition, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_between democracy [supported by the Athenians] The Corcyrian sedition arose from private grudges and the struggle between oligarchic supporters of the Lacedaemonians and democrats favoring Athens. The democrats killed or imprisoned opponents and expelled more than a thousand, but a later armed clash ended in pacification.

l: Conon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Conon is an Athenian admiral and commander whose career moves from leading Athens’s fleet to commanding Persia’s navy in ways intended to restore Athens’s power at sea. Chosen among ten Athenian commanders, he received the fleet from Alcibiades, assembled seventy ships, aided Methymna, and fought near Mitylene before withdrawing into the city with forty ships. Sharing command with Philocles, he escaped the defeat at Aegos Potamos and fled to Evagoras in Cyprus. While serving there, he was appointed Persian admiral at Pharnabazus’s recommendation. He commanded fleets at Caunus and elsewhere, gained Rhodes’s support, promised Artaxerxes to ruin the Lacedaemonian fleet, and jointly commanded with Pharnabazus. Their victory at Cnidus enabled him to win over cities and islands, sail to the Piraeus, help rebuild Athens’s walls, make a league with Corinth, and return to Asia.

l: Battle of Cyzicum, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a battle [at sea and on land between Athenians and Peloponnesians] In the Battle of Cyzicum, Alcibiades drew Mindarus's ships away from the city while Theramenes and Thrasybulus blocked their return. The Athenians defeated the Peloponnesians, captured many ships and prisoners, and gained abundant spoils.

l: Claros, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: hosts_battle Battle of Claros [where the Lacedaemonians fled after the naval engagement] Claros was the coastal place where Mindarus fled after being cut off from Cyzicum. Pharnabazus's army was encamped there and supported the Peloponnesians against the Athenians.

l: Battle of Claros, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: A land battle began as Athenians tried to seize shore-forced Peloponnesian ships; after Persian forces broke and Mindarus died, Peloponnesians fled and Athens won.

l: Athenian fleet, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Athenian fleet, seventy-four ships at Dardanium, defeated an opposing fleet after Alcibiades arrived. It assembled at Sestos and Cardia, sailed to Cyzicum under Alcibiades, and captured the Peloponnesian fleet after victories at sea and land. Later, seventy sail under Theramenes served during Chalcedon’s siege and operations around several cities.

l: Peloponnesian fleet, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_commanded_by Mindarus [at Cyzicum] The Peloponnesian fleet fought the Athenians at Dardanium under Mindarus and later assembled for operations from Abydos. It was drawn away from Cyzicum, defeated at sea and on land, and largely captured or driven off.

l: Pharnabazus's army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: supports Peloponnesians [from land at Claros] Pharnabazus's army supported the Peloponnesians at Dardanium and Claros. At Claros it fought from the shore and initially inflicted heavy losses on the Athenians, but it eventually broke and withdrew.

l: Endius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Endius, chief Spartan ambassador, led an embassy to Athens, spoke briefly in Laconic style, argued the war harmed Athenians most, and presented Spartan peace terms.

l: Cleophon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Cleophon opposes peace in the Athenian assembly, magnifying recent victories and urging confidence that fortune will preserve Athenian gains.

l: peace, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_proposed_on the peace terms [by the Lacedaemonians] The Spartans sought peace with Athens, but the Athenians refused after Cleophon encouraged confidence in their recent successes.

l: the rout at Cyzicum, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The rout at Cyzicum was confirmed to the Spartans and led them to send an embassy to Athens seeking peace.

l: the peace terms, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The proposed peace terms let each side keep gained cities, required all garrisons dismissed, and exchanged prisoners one Athenian for one Lacedaemonian.

l: the Athenians' victories, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: inflate Athenians [making them confident of recovering their former reputation] The Athenians' recent victories were emphasized by Cleophon, who used them to encourage rejection of peace. The Athenians consequently became confident that they would soon recover their former esteem and reputation.

l: Gelians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Gelians dedicate Apollo’s brazen statue, join Dionysius as an allied Sicilian city, fiercely defend Gela against siege, briefly aid Italians, then angered by Dionysius depart for Leontium.

l: the siege of Selinus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a siege [conducted by Hannibal against Selinus] The siege began after Hannibal landed in Sicily and marched from Lilybaeum toward Selinus. Hannibal used towers, battering rams, archers, and fresh troops in repeated assaults until breaches were opened and the Carthaginians captured the city.

l: the fall and destruction of Selinus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a destruction [following Hannibal's capture of the city] After Selinus fell, the Carthaginians killed inhabitants, plundered houses, burned or demolished buildings, and destroyed the city. Sixteen thousand people were killed and more than five thousand were taken captive, while Agrigentum received about twenty-five hundred refugees.

l: destruction of Himera, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: ends_with destruction of Himera [after the city's defenses are breached] Hannibal besieged Himera with Carthaginian and Sicilian forces, battering and undermining its walls. After the defenders were defeated and the city was entered, Hannibal ordered the inhabitants' slaughter to stop, but the city was plundered, its temples were burned, and Himera was razed.

l: the Battle of Himera, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a battle [in which the Himerians initially defeat the Carthaginian forces] The Himerians and their allies made a sudden sortie against the Carthaginian army and initially routed it, killing thousands. Hannibal brought reinforcements from the camp, defeated the Himerians in a second engagement, and three thousand Himerians died after making a determined stand.

l: the Carthaginian invasion of Sicily, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: includes the siege and destruction of Himera Hannibal began the Carthaginian invasion of Sicily by bringing an army from Spain and Africa aboard warships and transports. The invasion resulted in the capture and destruction of Selinus and Himera before Hannibal withdrew to Carthage with booty.

l: the Carthaginian army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Carthaginian army, reported by Ephorus as two hundred thousand foot and four thousand horse, used siege towers, battering rams, archers, and fresh troops to overcome Selinus and Himera. After damaging suburbs and plundering temples, it was devastated by plague, leaving it unable to care for the sick.

l: siege engines, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_located_in Syracuse [first known there] The art of making engines for hurling large stones was first practiced at Syracuse during Dionysius's preparations. He ordered artillery engines of many designs, and later used them in the approaches against Motya.

l: Chalcedon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: pays_tribute_to Athenians [the same tribute paid before, under terms arranged by Theramenes] Chalcedon was besieged by Theramenes with an Athenian force. After Hippocrates was killed in a sortie, Theramenes reached an agreement with the Chalcedonians that they would pay the same tribute as before.

l: Chrysopolis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a city [of Chalcedonia] Chrysopolis, a city of Chalcedonia, was the place where the surviving Greeks eventually arrived after crossing Bithynia. Only three thousand eight hundred of the original ten thousand were said to remain when they reached it.

l: Lampsacus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Lampsacus, a city, was besieged and captured by Lysander, whose forces dismissed its garrison, plundered it, restored it, and executed Philocles there.

l: war against the Athenians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The war continued with shifting fortunes at sea and on land. The Lacedaemonians rebuilt their naval power under Lysander with support from Cyrus, while the Athenians recalled Alcibiades, later removed him, and appointed Conon as admiral.

l: Hermocrates’s banishment, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_opposed_by Syracusans [the people later signaled their desire for recall] Hermocrates’s banishment was imposed by a contrary faction at home after he had served as admiral. It prevented his immediate return to Syracuse, but his later military successes caused the Syracusans to regret it and consider recalling him.

l: siege of Chalcedon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_conducted_by Theramenes [with Athenian forces] The siege of Chalcedon was conducted by Theramenes with an Athenian fleet and army. The Athenians built a timber wall from sea to sea, defeated a sortie led by Hippocrates, and then reached an agreement under which Chalcedon paid its previous tribute.

l: betrayal of Byzantium, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_carried_out_by Byzantines [inhabitants discontented with Clearchus's rigid government] The betrayal of Byzantium was carried out by some Byzantines who disliked Clearchus's harsh government. They helped Alcibiades's soldiers enter the city while the Peloponnesians were drawn toward the harbor, and the Athenians then took control after promising that the Byzantines would not be harmed.

l: Lysander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Lysander was a Spartan commander and bold, daring admiral of the Lacedaemonians. He assembled fleets and forces at Rhodes, Ephesus, Miletus, and Chios, receiving money from Cyrus for the army and the Lacedaemonian war. After defeating the Athenian fleet at Notium, he was discharged from an earlier command and handed the fleet at Ephesus to Callicratides. Later made high admiral, he raised ships, captured Lampsacus, defeated and captured the Athenian fleet at Aegos Potamos, took Sestos, and blockaded Samos and Athens. Following the war, he helped impose an oligarchic government at Athens, advised the selection of thirty governors, and held authority to establish oligarchies and settle city governments. Prominent at Sparta, he sought to end Heraclid rule and make any Spartan eligible for kingship, unsuccessfully trying to bribe oracles. Summoned to Athens with ships and soldiers, he faced Pausanias's opposition. Finally sent to Phocis, he besieged Haliartus and was killed there in battle.

l: Diomedon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Diomedon, an excellent, just, virtuous soldier and condemned commander, urged Athenians to thank Jove, Apollo, and the goddesses for victory before Athenian execution.

l: Notium, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Notium was the place where the Athenian fleet anchored while Alcibiades went elsewhere with several ships. A naval battle occurred nearby, in which Lysander defeated the Athenians and destroyed or captured twenty-two of their ships.

l: battle of Notium, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The battle of Notium began when Antiochus, contrary to Alcibiades's orders, challenged the Lacedaemonians. Lysander sank Antiochus's ship, routed the remaining advance vessels, and defeated the Athenian fleet with the loss of twenty-two ships.

l: Athenian assembly, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: condemns Athenian commanders [to death for failure to bury the dead] The Athenian assembly initially applauded the commanders for the victory but became angry over the failure to bury the dead. It allowed the accusations to prevail, prevented the accused from being heard amid a tumult, and condemned the commanders to death.

l: Athenian fleet, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Athenian fleet returned to Athens with about two hundred captured ships, prisoners, and rich spoils. It later suffered defeat at Notium after Antiochus engaged Lysander without waiting for Alcibiades, and Alcibiades ultimately surrendered command of it to Conon.

l: Spartan fleet, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Spartan fleet was rebuilt after losses and Mindarus's death, funded by Cyrus and led by Lysander to victory at Notium. Under Callicratides, it grew to 150 ships, defeated Conon near Mitylene, then, with 140 ships, suffered major losses at Arginusae and fled.

l: Callicratides, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Callicratides is a Lacedaemonian admiral and general, esteemed among the Spartans for justice, integrity, and a plain, honest character. Appointed after Lysander and given a fleet of 150 ships, he took Methymna, besieged and surrounded Mitylene, and defeated Athenians in the harbour. Foreseeing death, he named Clearchus successor, fought at Arginusae, damaged enemy ships, and died when Athenians boarded his vessel.

l: siege of Mitylene, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The siege of Mitylene followed a naval engagement: Callicratides, having taken the harbour outside the walls, landed troops and besieged the defended city on every side. Eteonicus maintained the siege while Callicratides sailed away, then withdrew the forces after learning of defeat.

l: naval battle at Mitylene, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_fought_at harbour at Mitylene [between Conon and Callicratides] Conon initially attacked part of Callicratides' larger fleet near Mitylene after drawing its leading ships away from the rest. Callicratides eventually brought the whole fleet together, forced Conon into the inner harbour, and gained control of the harbour outside the city walls.

l: Hermocrates' attempted return to Syracuse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_defeated_at Syracuse [discovered by the Syracusans] Hermocrates returned from Selinus with three thousand armed men after being summoned by members of his faction. His plan was discovered, the Syracusans assembled in arms, and Hermocrates and many accomplices were killed; the surviving participants were condemned to banishment.

l: harbour at Mitylene, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: lies_outside Mitylene [between the old city and the mainland addition] Conon blocked the harbour entrance with stone-filled vessels and ships fixed by anchors, while defending the shallows and the open passage. Callicratides eventually drove the Athenians from their position, entered the harbour, and anchored close to Mitylene.

l: Agrigentum campaign, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Agrigentum campaign was a Carthaginian siege of Agrigentum, driven by the city’s position and wealth. Agrigentines stored food and valuables and rejected alliance or neutrality proposals. Despite allied aid, Carthaginian siege works, destruction of the Syracusan grain fleet, and famine forced the defenders to withdraw.

l: the peace between Carthage and Dionysius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: ends the first Carthaginian war against Dionysius The peace between Carthage and Dionysius gave the Carthaginians power over the Sicanians, Selinuntines, Agrigentines, and Himeraeans. Gela and Camarina could remain inhabited without walls but had to pay tribute, while Leontium, Messania, and the other Sicilians retained their laws and liberties; the Syracusans remained subject to Dionysius.

l: Carthaginian invasion of Sicily, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Carthaginians prepared an invasion of Sicily by raising a very large army and assembling warships and transport vessels. Their first fleet action near Eryx ended with fifteen Carthaginian ships sunk, but Hannibal sailed afterward to support the planned crossing.

l: Carthaginian army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: has_reported_strength 120000 men [according to Timaeus] The Carthaginian army was recruited from Carthaginians, Africans, Spaniards, Balearic islanders, allied Mauretanians and Numidians, people near Cyrene, and Campanians hired from Italy. Timaeus estimated it at somewhat more than 120,000 men, while Ephorus gave a figure of 300,000.

l: Syracusan fleet, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: includes warships [including ships with three and five oars on a bank] Dionysius built more than two hundred galleys, refitted one hundred and ten, and repaired or covered one hundred and fifty older vessels. A Carthaginian night raid in the harbor of Syracuse destroyed almost all the ships stationed there.

l: Grecians in Italy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Grecians in Italy were Greek forces from Italy in Dionysius's army. They fought near Gela, were overwhelmed with heavy losses, and left his camp for home. Separately, their confederate forces opposed Lucanians and Dionysius, but premature action and later defeat at Helorus ruined them.

l: Gellias, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Gellias, a wealthy Agrigentine known for integrity and ingenuity, generously housed, fed, and clothed strangers and horsemen despite a mean appearance; he later died in Minerva after setting fire to the temple.

l: temple of Jupiter Olympus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The temple of Jupiter Olympus at Agrigentum, Sicily’s largest temple, was built with lofty outer pillars, foursquare inner pillars, walls, and carvings of the giants’ war and Troy. Near completion, war halted construction; after the city was sacked, it remained unfinished.

l: Agrigentum's temples, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The temples of Agrigentum, especially the temple of Jupiter, testified to the grandeur and wealth of the city’s people. Most of the other sacred buildings had been burned or destroyed by repeated storming of the city.

l: Agrigentines' wealth and luxury, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: includes gold and silver vessels [water pots and boxes of ointment] Agrigentines’ wealth came partly from vineyards, olive groves, and the sale of olives to Carthage, and it was displayed in temples, tombs, chariots, gold clothing, and gold and silver vessels. Their luxurious habits extended to public feasts, weddings, hospitality, and military life, where even basic restrictions on guards’ sleeping arrangements were resented.

l: Amilcar the Carthaginian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Amilcar the Carthaginian is a Carthaginian general who commanded with Hannibal at Agrigentum and later commanded the Carthaginians after Hannibal’s death. During the siege he ordered assaults and siege works, sacrificed during plague, ambushed a Syracusan grain fleet, and plundered Agrigentum. He then devastated Gela and Camarina, marched against Gela, and made peace with Dionysius.

l: Dexippus the Lacedaemonian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Dexippus, a Lacedaemonian living at Gela, aided Agrigentum by bringing five hundred soldiers and directing its defense. He later joined a war council, where he was accused of treachery and of accepting fifteen talents to urge Italian commanders to withdraw.

l: Daphnaeus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: A Syracusan general appointed to command the relief army for Agrigentum, Daphnaeus led forces from several cities, defeated the Carthaginian army after it crossed the Himera, occupied its former camp, and restrained pursuit.

l: Battle of the Himera, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Battle of the Himera was a battle near the Himera River in which Daphnaeus led the Syracusans against Carthaginian forces and allies. After a long engagement, the Syracusans won, routing the army, killing over six thousand soldiers, and pursuing survivors to camp.

l: Carthaginian naval attack on the Syracusan grain fleet, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: sink eight ships [of the Syracusan fleet] Amilcar sent forty galleys from Panormus and Motya to ambush the Syracusan ships carrying grain to Agrigentum. The Carthaginians sank eight ships and drove the rest ashore, capturing the fleet and transforming the situation in their favor.

l: Agrigentum's fall, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Agrigentum's fall followed famine and the departure of allied forces, which weakened defenders and inhabitants and caused evacuation. Amilcar entered the abandoned city, killed nearly all he found, and destroyed or removed its wealth. The fall spread terror, drove refugees to Syracuse or Italy, and intensified political accusations.

l: the plague in the Carthaginian army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: A plague raged in Africa and the Carthaginian army after temples of Ceres and Proserpina were plundered. Heat, crowding, marshes, and unburied bodies intensified it, causing severe illnesses and rapid deaths, killing many soldiers and leaving Carthage unprepared for Dionysius's attack.

l: evacuation of Agrigentum, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Evacuation of Agrigentum began when insufficient provisions prompted departure; guarded refugees reached Gela, then Leontium, while the sick and elderly were abandoned and some inhabitants killed themselves.

l: the sack of Agrigentum, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The sack of Agrigentum, carried out by Amilcar after the city was abandoned, saw remaining inhabitants killed, even in temples, and religious and secular places plundered; treasures and finest spoils were sent to Carthage.

l: Syracusan grain fleet, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: carry grain [for the besieged at Agrigentum] The Syracusan grain fleet carried abundant corn intended for Agrigentum. It was attacked unexpectedly by Amilcar's forty galleys in winter; eight ships were sunk and the remainder were driven ashore and captured.

l: exiles, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The exiles are recalled to Syracuse to help defend the country; Dionysius views them as changeable tools for his ambition, and they return after the decree.

l: the war against Carthage, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The war against Carthage brought fear, accusations, and military preparations to Syracuse. Dionysius used the threat to recall exiles, raise soldiers’ pay, and gain sole command; despite calls to remove him, he attacked a plague-weakened Carthaginian army, took forts, and destroyed much of its fleet.

l: Dionysius's seizure of power, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Dionysius seized power in Syracuse by accusing rivals, controlling soldiers, building a personal guard, recruiting supporters, removing opponents, and openly declaring himself king, establishing tyranny.

l: tyranny, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Syracusans recognized that granting Dionysius sole command would lead to tyranny, although they had helped create the situation. Dionysius then used his guard, mercenaries, political alliances, and control of the city to establish himself as ruler.

l: battle of Arginusae, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: A sea battle near Arginusae pitted 150 Athenian ships against 140 Lacedaemonian ships; Athens won despite losing twenty-five ships to seventy-seven Peloponnesian losses.

l: Pericles the younger, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: commands Athenian fleet [right wing at Arginusae] Pericles the younger commanded the Athenian right wing with Thrasybulus. His ship engaged Callicratides’s vessel, which became fixed to it, allowing the Athenians to board and kill those aboard.

l: Arginusae, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Arginusae are islands between Mitylene and Cuma near Catanides, inhabited by Aeolians with a small town, where the Athenian fleet returned after a storm.

l: the Thirty Tyrants of Athens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Thirty Tyrants were an oligarchic government, nominally magistrates but actually usurping tyrants, appointed after pressure to abolish democracy. They staffed offices with supporters, sought a Lacedaemonian garrison, banished and executed Athenians, and confiscated property, until Thrasybulus's forces expelled them and a decemvirate replaced them.

l: Athenian commanders, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: are_accused_of failure to bury the dead [after the battle of Arginusae] The Athenian commanders arranged their fleet for battle and helped secure the victory at Arginusae. Eleven of them were later condemned to death and had their estates confiscated because the dead were not buried, although the storm had prevented that duty.

l: Arginusae commanders’ trial and execution, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: results_in execution of eleven commanders [by lawful officers] The commanders were ordered to return to Athens and were tried after the people heard accusations supported by the relatives of the dead. Eleven commanders were condemned to death, and they were led to execution despite having won the greatest sea-fight described as fought by Grecians against Grecians.

l: failure to bury the dead, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_caused_by storm at Arginusae [the storm and battle damage delayed recovery] The dead could not be recovered because a violent storm shattered the ships and prevented the Athenians from reaching Mitylene or carrying out the burial. The failure nevertheless led to the commanders’ prosecution and execution at Athens.

l: Athenian fleet, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Athenian fleet began with 150 ships from Athenians, other islands, and Samians. It won at Arginusae but lost twenty-five ships and most aboard them. Later it had 173 ships at Samos, left twenty there, sailed toward the Hellespont, assembled 180 ships, and was captured at Aegos Potamos.

l: storm at Arginusae, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: prevents failure to bury the dead [the storm prevented recovery of the bodies] A violent storm arose after the battle and greatly damaged the ships. It prevented the Athenians from recovering the dead or sailing directly to Mitylene, forcing them back to Arginusae.

l: victory at Arginusae, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a Athenian victory The Athenians achieved a decisive victory at Arginusae after Callicratides was killed and the Lacedaemonian fleet fled. The victory was later overshadowed by the execution of the Athenian commanders for the failure to bury the dead.

l: Aegos Potamos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a anchorage [where the Athenian fleet lay after Lampsacus was taken] Aegos Potamos was the place where the Athenian fleet anchored after the Athenians learned that Lampsacus had fallen. Lysander later surprised the fleet there and captured nearly all of its ships.

l: Evagoras, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Evagoras, a noble Cypriot prince descended from Salamis’s founders, returned with a small band, expelled Abdemon the Tyrian, became king of Salamis, gained cities by force or promises, and sought dominion over all Cyprus, prompting appeals to Artaxerxes.

l: Thurians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Thurians responded to a Lucanian incursion by marching against the enemy with more than fourteen thousand foot soldiers and a thousand horsemen, without waiting for their confederates. They entered Lucania, were surrounded and defeated, and suffered heavy losses.

l: Aegeospotami naval battle, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a Athenian naval defeat [with Lysander capturing the Athenian fleet] At the Aegeospotami naval battle, Lysander exploited the disorder of the Athenian fleet and captured its ships after a brief resistance. Conon and a few other commanders escaped, while Philocles was taken prisoner and executed.

l: capture of Lampsacus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a Lacedaemonian victory [Lysander took the city by siege or storm] The capture of Lampsacus was carried out by Lysander after he assembled a large navy. He dismissed the Athenian garrison, plundered the city, and restored it to its inhabitants.

l: siege of Athens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a Lacedaemonian blockade [forcing Athens into extreme want of food] The siege of Athens followed the defeat of the Athenian fleet. Agis and Pausanias invaded Attica while Lysander entered the Piraeus with more than two hundred ships, and the blockade caused severe famine in the city.

l: surrender of Athens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a peace settlement [demolishing the fortifications and limiting the fleet] The surrender of Athens occurred after famine caused many deaths in the city. Athens agreed to demolish its walls and the long fortifications of the Piraeus, keep no more than ten long ships, leave the other cities, and become subject to the Lacedaemonians.

l: the Sicilians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Sicilians, soldiers in Dionysius's garrison and army, fiercely assaulted Motya, suffered heavy losses, then entered, killed inhabitants and plundered wealth despite Dionysius's order to spare prisoners.

l: mercenary soldiers, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Mercenary soldiers serve and guard Dionysius, supporting him against opposition. Dionysius sends a thousand with horsemen against the Carthaginian camp, then abandons them to be killed. Distrusting the survivors under Aristotle, he seizes their general, pays about ten thousand with Leontium, and recruits more mercenaries.

l: Camarina, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_tributary_to the Carthaginians [under the peace settlement and without walls] Camarina was devastated by Amilcar's forces.
