Dionysius later ordered its citizens, including their wives and children, to remove to Syracuse, and the people of Camarina subsequently became hostile to him and turned toward Leontium.

l: the first Carthaginian war against Dionysius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: occurs_in Sicily The first Carthaginian war against Dionysius ended after Amilcar's campaign against Gela, Dionysius's failed relief effort, and the unrest that followed his withdrawal. Peace was made with several cities placed under Carthaginian power or tribute and Syracuse left subject to Dionysius.

l: the siege of Gela, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: During the siege of Gela, the Gelians defended their damaged walls, sent out troops against Carthaginian stragglers, and worked through the night to repair breaches. Dionysius eventually came with a large army, but the relief attack failed and he withdrew, after which the Carthaginians entered and plundered the city.

l: the battle before Gela, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: In the battle before Gela, the Italians attacked the Carthaginian camp near the shore, while the Sicilians attacked elsewhere and Dionysius's mercenaries attempted to reach the Carthaginian engines. The Italians were driven back with heavy losses, the Sicilians also retreated after losing six hundred men, and Dionysius withdrew into Gela before abandoning the city.

l: the oligarchy of Athens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_supported_by Lysander [after the Peloponnesian War] The supporters of oligarchy in Athens appealed to Lysander to restore an earlier form of government. The oligarchy was established through the appointment of the Thirty, who ruled with the support of Lacedaemonian power.

l: the peace between Athens and Sparta, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The peace required Athens to demolish its walls and govern according to the laws of its own country. Lysander claimed that the Athenians had broken the agreement by failing to pull down their walls within the stipulated time.

l: the Thirty's government of Athens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: administers Athens [through thirty governors] The Thirty were charged with choosing the senate, creating magistrates, and making laws, but they delayed making laws while placing their supporters in offices. They brought in a foreign garrison, killed opponents and wealthy citizens, seized estates, and caused many inhabitants to flee.

l: Critias, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Critias, the president of the Thirty, accused Theramenes before the senate of betraying the government. When Theramenes cleared himself and gained the senate's approval, Critias ordered soldiers to seize him. Critias commanded the Thirty Tyrants' attack on Munychia. He was killed during the sharp engagement, after which the tyrants' forces withdrew.

l: the Thirty's execution of Theramenes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Thirty had Theramenes dragged from the senate-house altar by the lictors and led through the marketplace to execution. The people lamented his fate but did not rescue him because armed soldiers surrounded him.

l: the Athenian exiles, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Athenian exiles gathered around Thrasybulus and grew numerous after his successes. They helped defeat the tyrants, seized the Piraeus, besieged Athens, and were eventually restored to their country.

l: the Thirty Years' tyranny in Athens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The tyranny of the Thirty grew increasingly violent after its rulers secured a Lacedaemonian garrison. They executed prominent and wealthy citizens, confiscated their estates, and reduced Athens so severely that more than half of its inhabitants fled.

l: the Syracusan siege of Dionysius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Syracusans and their allies camped at the Epipolae, blocked Dionysius's passage, and attacked the island daily with siege engines. The siege weakened when Dionysius obtained Campanian aid, after which he sallied out and defeated the divided Syracusans.

l: Coronea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a site of a battle [between Agesilaus and the Boeotians and their confederates] Coronea was the site of a battle between Agesilaus and the Boeotians and their confederates. The Boeotians defeated the opposing Lacedaemonian wing, while Agesilaus routed the other part.

l: the Spartan kingship, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_held_by the Heraclidae [before Lysander's proposed reform] Lysander sought to change the Spartan kingship so that the king could be chosen from any Spartan family rather than only from the families of the Heraclidae. He attempted to secure support for this plan by bribing several oracles, without success.

l: the Elei, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: are_at_war_with the Lacedaemonians [after refusing Spartan demands] The Elei refused the Lacedaemonians' demands that neighboring cities govern themselves and contribute to the costs of the war against the Athenians. They defended their city with help from citizens and Etolian soldiers, killed about thirty of Pausanias's men in a sortie, and endured the destruction of their countryside.

l: the Epipolae fortification, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: A fortification at Epipolae with six gates, towers, and a thirty-furlong wall, ordered by Dionysius and completed in twenty days by sixty thousand freemen and six thousand yoke of oxen.

l: the war between Dionysius and Carthage, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The war was planned by Dionysius after securing Sicily and making peace, secretly preparing by fortifying Epipolae. It unfolded through invasion of Carthaginian territories, the siege of Egesta, capture of Motya, destruction of Messana, and naval battle of Catana. Carthaginian victories brought fighting to Syracuse, where Dionysius defended with fortified positions, recruits, and foreign assistance.

l: the war against the Elei, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Lacedaemonians used complaints about the Elei's treatment of Pausanias and their exclusion of Spartans from the Olympic games as pretexts for war. Pausanias invaded Elis, captured several places, but failed to conquer the city and spent the winter in Dyme.

l: war between Cyrus and Artaxerxes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a war [between brothers] The war arose from Cyrus's attempt to seize the Persian kingdom from his brother Artaxerxes. Cyrus marched through Asia and across the Euphrates, while Artaxerxes gathered a much larger army and met him near Babylon. Cyrus was killed in the battle, and Artaxerxes's forces ultimately prevailed.

l: Grecian forces, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Grecian forces were Lacedaemonians and other Greek mercenaries serving under Cyrus. They defeated Artaxerxes’s army on Clearchus’s wing and routed opposing forces, then repelled attack after Cyrus’s death. Refusing to surrender, they made a truce, replaced massacred commanders under Chirosophus, fought through hostile countries, reached the sea, recovered from honey poisoning, passed Bithynia, and arrived at Chrysopolis with 3,800 survivors.

l: march out of Persia into Greece, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Cyrus's army made a long and difficult march from Asia toward Babylon, passing through Cilicia, Syria, and the narrow gates and mountain passes on the way. The soldiers feared the reported distance to Bactria and the many hostile nations along the route, but continued after Cyrus promised them increased pay and rewards.

l: Chirosophus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Chirosophus, a Lacedaemonian general and intimate friend of Anaxibius, commanded eight hundred soldiers sent to support Cyrus and delivered them at Issus. After Greek commanders were massacred, soldiers chose him as general; he sought ships at Byzantium but returned without them.

l: Tamos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: commands barbarian fleet [as admiral] Tamos, the chief lord-lieutenant of Ionia, feared Tissaphernes and fled to Egypt with his wealth and children, except Gaus. Psammetichus murdered Tamos, his children, and his attendants to obtain their money and ships.

l: Tissaphernes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Tissaphernes is a noble Persian, Artaxerxes’s faithful friend and relative by marriage, who becomes governor and lieutenant of the sea-coast provinces formerly under Cyrus. When Artaxerxes is wounded in battle, he takes command, rallies the soldiers, fights bravely, and kills many of Cyrus’s men. Rewarded as the bravest man, he receives authority to pursue the Greeks, seizes Clearchus and other commanders by treachery, and attacks the retreating Greeks. He then threatens Cyrus’s supporters, attacks the Cumeans, and joins Pharnabazus in raising forces against the Lacedaemonians. Commanding a vast army against Agesilaus, he is defeated near Sipylus, flees to Sardis, and is seized and executed by Artaxerxes as the alleged cause of the war.

l: the battle of Cunaxa, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: A battle near Babylon between Cyrus's Greek-supported army and Artaxerxes's Persian forces. The Grecians routed their opponents and Clearchus's men inflicted most royal casualties, but Cyrus was killed after striking Artaxerxes. The royalists overcame Cyrus's main army, and the Grecians later defeated barbarians attacking after nightfall; Artaxerxes won.

l: Cyrus's army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: has_strength eighty-three thousand men [seventy thousand from Asia and thirteen thousand Greek mercenaries] Cyrus's army consisted of about seventy thousand men from Asia, thirteen thousand Greek mercenaries, and additional forces gathered during the march. It crossed the Euphrates and fought Artaxerxes's much larger army, but lost its leader and was ultimately defeated, although the Greek contingent remained victorious in its own engagements.

l: Artaxerxes's army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Artaxerxes's army, an army assembled from many regions, was estimated by Ephorus at at least four hundred thousand horse and foot. It first lost to the Grecians, then, after Cyrus's death, recovered, plundered his camp, defeated his main forces, attacked stragglers under Tissaphernes, and pursued the Greeks to the Carduchi without facing their whole army.

l: Greek mercenaries, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Greek mercenaries were about thirteen thousand experienced soldiers from the Peloponnesus and other parts of Greece. Commanded in separate contingents by Clearchus, Proxenus, Socrates, and Menon, they repeatedly routed less experienced barbarians. Under Clearchus and Aridaeus, they became the principal Greek force in the retreat, permitted peaceful passage through the king's territory if they committed no outrages.

l: Aridaeus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: commands the mercenaries [jointly with Clearchus] After Cyrus's death, Aridaeus returned to his former post and asked Clearchus to join forces with him near the sea. He was included with the mercenaries whose peaceful passage was promised, but Tissaphernes later used him as part of the scheme to destroy the Greeks.

l: the Carduchi, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Carduchi are a free, warlike people independent of and hostile to the king, skilled in mountain warfare; using slings and powerful bows, they attack Greeks from higher ground, causing many deaths and wounds.

l: the country of the Carduchi, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_crossed_by the Greeks [over seven days] The Greeks reached the country of the Carduchi after Tissaphernes pursued them. They suffered attacks from the inhabitants for seven days while crossing its mountains before reaching the river Centrites.

l: Trapezus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Trapezus, a Greek city, was a Sinopian colony belonging to the Colchians; after Clearchus slaughtered many, Greeks stayed thirty days, received hospitality, sacrificed, held games, and obtained two small vessels.

l: Cyrus's expedition against Artaxerxes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Cyrus's expedition against Artaxerxes ended with Cyrus's death and the defeat of his forces. The surviving Greeks then began their long retreat toward the sea and eventually returned toward their own country.

l: the Greek retreat, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Greek retreat proceeded through the country of the Carduchi, Armenia, the lands of the Chaonians, Phasians, Chalcidonians, Tascutians, Macrones, Colchians, and others. The Greeks faced hostile inhabitants, difficult mountains, winter storms, shortages, and repeated attacks before reaching Greek cities and eventually Chrysopolis.

l: the commanders' massacre, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a betrayal [by Tissaphernes] Tissaphernes summoned Clearchus and the other Greek commanders to his tent under the pretense of discussion. After a purple flag was raised, the commanders were seized, those outside were killed, and the captured commanders were sent in chains to Artaxerxes, who put them to death except Menon.

l: the crossing of the Carduchian mountains, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: lasts seven days [the Greeks suffered attacks from the inhabitants] The Greeks spent seven days crossing the mountains of the Carduchi and suffered heavily from attacks by the inhabitants. The Carduchi used elevated positions, slings, and unusually large bows and arrows against them.

l: the Armenian snowstorm, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: causes severe hardship [the army is immobilized by snow, cold, wind, and hail] While crossing the Armenian mountains, the Greeks encountered deep snow, freezing cold, hail, and violent wind. They were forced to remain where the storm found them, losing men, animals, and the use of some fingers and toes before reaching villages with underground shelters and supplies.

l: the honey poisoning, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: In the country of the Colchians, many Greeks ate honeycombs and immediately became mad and lay on the ground as if dead. By the same hour the next day they recovered their senses and strength, and three days later the army reached Trapezus.

l: Phila, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Phila was a very strong castle about one hundred stages from Athens. Thrasybulus secretly seized it with assistance from Thebes, giving the exiles a position from which Attica could easily be invaded.

l: Thimbron, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Thimbron was a Lacedaemonian general appointed by the Lacedaemonians to wage war against the Persian king in Asia. With Spartan and allied troops, he reached Ephesus, took Magnesia, failed at Tralles, and withdrew before Tissaphernes. Later he occupied Jonda and Corossus, but Struthius surprised and killed him during a plundering expedition.

l: the war against the Persian king, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a war [conducted in defence of the Greek cities] The war against the Persian king began as a Lacedaemonian response to Persian attacks on the Greek cities of Asia. Thimbron first led the campaign, and Dercyllidas was later sent to replace him because the war was being badly managed.

l: Dercyllidas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Dercyllidas was sent by the Lacedaemonians to replace Thimbron as general in Asia. He quickly captured cities in the territory of Troas, fought the Thracians in Bithynia, later expelled them from the Chersonesus of Thrace, and returned to Asia.

l: the Chersonesus of Thrace, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Chersonesus of Thrace was invaded and ravaged by large bodies of Thracians, who seized its fortified cities. Dercyllidas drove them out and built a wall from one sea to the other, protecting the region from further incursions.

l: the Persian fleet, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Persian fleet was planned and equipped after Pharnabazus persuaded the king to continue preparations for war. Conon was appointed its admiral, though he initially sailed with only forty ships to Cilicia because the full fleet was not ready.

l: Lacedaemonian fleet, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The Lacedaemonian fleet, an eighty-five-galley force under Pisander, operated from Rhodes and sought to besiege Caunus under Pharax; Conon gained Persian support against it, and near Cnidus it was defeated, losing ships, prisoners, and sovereignty of the sea.

l: Socrates' trial and execution, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Socrates' trial and execution followed accusations by Anytus and Melitus that he was an atheist and corrupted the youth. After Socrates was put to death by poison, the Athenians regretted the decision and killed his accusers without waiting for legal formalities.

l: the Athenian restoration, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: restores the Athenian citizens [to their country and ancient laws] The Athenian restoration followed Pausanias's intervention after the exiles had taken the Piraeus and the city had expelled the Thirty Tyrants. The exiles and citizens were reconciled, Athens resumed government according to its ancient laws, and those fearing punishment could withdraw to Eleusis.

l: Rhegians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Rhegians, related to Naxians and Cataneans, feared Dionysius after their enslavement, tried war with Syracusan exiles, withdrew after Messanian mutiny, then made peace.

l: war between the Rhegians and Dionysius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a war The Rhegians initiated preparations for war against Dionysius because they feared suffering the same fate as the Naxians and Cataneans. The campaign ended without a battle after the Messanian soldiers rejected their commanders and returned home, prompting the Rhegians to withdraw and later seek peace.

l: war between Carthage and Syracuse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: War between Carthage and Syracuse began as Dionysius raised forces, built ships and weapons, sought allies, and demanded restoration of Greek cities. He marched on Eryx and Motya; Himiico tried to relieve Motya, but Dionysius captured and garrisoned it, then sent Leptinos to watch Carthage and raid Egesta and Entella.

l: siege of Motya, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: The siege of Motya was Dionysius’s campaign against the resisting Motyans after most nearby Sicilian cities had submitted. He filled the channel to approach the island, built a rampart, and used rams, engines, and six-floored towers. After several days of assault, his army entered through a passage seized at night.

l: Himilco, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Himilco was a Carthaginian king and general appointed under Carthaginian law. He led the campaign against Dionysius, capturing Motya and Messana, defeating the Sicilian fleet near Catana, and besieging Syracuse. Disease afflicted his forces; after their defeat, he paid Dionysius’s agents, escaped to Carthage with few survivors, lived in disgrace, and killed himself in poverty.

l: Veii, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: is_a city [where many Romans who escaped the defeat took refuge] Many Romans who escaped the defeat at the Allia fled to Veii and fortified it. From Veii they attacked the Tuscans, recovered arms and plunder, assembled additional forces, and planned to relieve the Capitol.

l: Carthaginian night raid on Syracuse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books
s: Himilco secretly sent an admiral with ten galleys to Syracuse, intending to destroy the ships in the harbor and force Dionysius to divide his forces. Entering at night, the admiral broke up, sank, and destroyed almost all the ships he found there before returning toward Carthage.
